stories.headline: APRIL CPI SURGES TO 3.8% — HIGHEST SINCE 2023 — AS IRAN OIL SHOCK DRIVES ENERGY +17.9% YoY
stories.body: April CPI rose 0.6% MoM (vs. consensus +0.3%) and 3.8% YoY, with energy accounting for over 40% of the headline gain. Core CPI held sticky at +2.8% YoY. S&P 500 fell 0.34%, the 10Y yield spiked 6 bps to 4.46%, and real average hourly wages slipped 0.5% for the month — the worst monthly real-wage print since the 2022 inflation peak.

stories.headline: TRUMP REJECTS IRAN PEACE OFFER; WTI SURGES TO $101.87 AS HORMUZ STANDOFF DRAGS INTO WEEK 12
stories.body: President Trump declared the US-Iran ceasefire on 'massive life support' after rejecting Tehran's latest proposal, sending WTI crude up 3.11% to $101.87 — the highest close since the Hormuz closure began. The IEA has called it the largest supply disruption in oil market history, with roughly 14.5M barrels per day offline and Brent prices up approximately 40% from pre-conflict levels.

stories.headline: TRUMP HEADS TO BEIJING MAY 14-15 FOR XI SUMMIT; TARIFF DEAL ODDS HOVER NEAR 50-50
stories.body: President Trump travels to Beijing Thursday for a two-day summit with Xi Jinping. Energy and agriculture deals are expected but a broader tariff agreement remains uncertain — Polymarket puts the odds of a US-China deal by May 31 at 49.5%. US-China merchandise trade has fallen more than one-third since peak tariff escalation, and both sides are managing expectations ahead of the meeting.

stories.headline: FED RATE HIKE ODDS JUMP TO 30% AFTER HOT CPI; RATE CUTS ENTIRELY OFF THE TABLE FOR 2026
stories.body: Today's CPI surprise closed the door on cuts and opened a crack toward hikes. CME FedWatch now prices a 30% probability of at least one Fed funds rate increase by year-end. Real average hourly wages are down 0.3% YoY — workers absorbing the oil shock for now — but the Fed's credibility anchor hinges on keeping 5Y5Y forward inflation expectations below the 2.5% threshold.

stories.headline: NCAA EXPANDS MARCH MADNESS TO 76 TEAMS STARTING 2027, ADDING SEVEN AT-LARGE BIDS
stories.body: The NCAA voted to expand the men's and women's basketball tournaments from 68 to 76 teams beginning in 2026-27, growing at-large selections from 37 to 44. Twelve additional games front-load the first week of the tournament. The expansion is bankrolled by roughly $300M in new sponsorships — including beer, wine, and spirits. Power conferences (ACC, Big 12, Big Ten, SEC) are projected to absorb most of the new spots.

stories.headline: MITCHELL TIES PLAYOFF HALF RECORD WITH 39 PTS IN 2ND HALF; CAVALIERS EVEN PISTONS SERIES 2-2
stories.body: Donovan Mitchell erupted for 43 total points — 39 in the second half alone, tying Eric 'Sleepy' Floyd's all-time playoff half-scoring mark — as Cleveland outlasted top-seeded Detroit 112-103 in Game 4 of the East Semifinals. The Cavs erased a double-digit deficit with a 22-0 third-quarter run. Game 5 is Wednesday in Detroit. In the West, OKC completed a sweep of the Lakers (SGA: 35 pts in Game 4) and is now 8-0 in these playoffs.

stories.headline: ROOKIE MINICAMPS UNDERWAY LEAGUEWIDE; 12 TOP-100 FREE AGENTS STILL UNSIGNED
stories.body: 2026 draft picks reported to facilities this week as teams launched rookie minicamps across the league. With the draft behind them, front offices are working the periphery — 12 of the offseason's top-100 free agents remain unsigned, expected to find homes ahead of or during training camp. The Seattle Seahawks signed veteran edge rusher Dante Fowler Jr. Monday, citing his relationship with DC Aden Durde as the deciding factor.

stories.headline: SPRING BALL COMPLETE NATIONALLY; OKLAHOMA STATE LEADS FBS WITH 50 INCOMING TRANSFERS UNDER ERIC MORRIS
stories.body: Spring practices have wrapped across the country with programs pivoting to summer conditioning. Oklahoma State brought in 50 transfer players under new head coach Eric Morris — the most of any FBS program in the 2026 cycle. Penn State's staff imported nearly 40 transfers from Iowa State. The spring transfer portal window was permanently eliminated after 2025; January now serves as the sole portal period.

deepDive.title: How Oil Shocks Pass Through to CPI — and Why the Fed Is Trapped
content: Today's April CPI print — 3.8% YoY, the highest since May 2023 — landed as a gut-punch to rate-cut hopes and pushed markets lower across the board. Energy was the proximate driver, rising 3.8% in a single month and 17.9% over the past year, accounting for over 40% of the headline gain. The proximate cause is the 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis, which the IEA has called the largest oil supply disruption in market history. With WTI at $101.87 and Trump rejecting Iran's latest peace proposal today, the transmission from geopolitics to the CPI basket is direct, sustained, and far from over.

There are two distinct channels through which oil prices feed into CPI. The first is direct: energy carries roughly a 7% weight in the headline basket, so a sustained 40% rise in energy prices mechanically contributes about 2.8 percentage points to headline inflation. The second channel is more insidious — oil is an input to nearly every production process. Trucking runs on diesel, airlines on jet fuel, plastics are petrochemical-derived. When crude surges, transport and input costs rise, and firms pass them downstream through higher prices. This second-round effect shows up in core goods and services with a 2–4 month lag, which is why core CPI of +2.8% YoY remains elevated even as the sharpest phase of the oil spike is relatively recent.

The historical precedent haunting the Fed is 1973–74. Chair Arthur Burns treated the Arab oil embargo as transitory and kept monetary policy accommodative. His critical error was allowing the shock to trigger second-round wage inflation — workers demanded cost-of-living adjustments, embedding oil-driven price increases into a self-reinforcing wage-price spiral. It took Paul Volcker's 20% federal funds rate in 1981 to break those expectations. The good news today is that real average hourly wages fell 0.5% in April and are down 0.3% YoY, meaning workers are absorbing the oil shock rather than demanding compensation. If that holds, the inflationary impulse stays supply-side and self-limiting. If it doesn't, the Fed faces the Volcker dilemma.

The Fed's structural problem is that a supply-side shock calls for patience — if Hormuz reopens, oil normalizes and CPI falls mechanically without a single rate hike. But a demand-side response (hikes) risks choking an economy that isn't overheating on the demand side at all. Markets have already moved: CME FedWatch now prices a 30% chance of a hike by year-end. The key forward indicator is the 5-year/5-year forward inflation breakeven rate, currently near 2.4% — if it cracks above 2.5%, the Fed loses its credibility anchor and feels compelled to act regardless of demand conditions. The Trump-Xi summit on May 14-15 adds a wildcard: a comprehensive energy or trade deal reducing inflationary pressure could give the Fed the economic cover it needs to hold rates unchanged through year-end.
